**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This one is about building and sustaining the *infrastructure* of ocean observation: deploying equipment, running observing-system experiments, network optimization, and technology roadmaps with industry. It's framed around the GOOS/IOC framework, Copernicus Marine Service, and areas beyond national jurisdiction. The emphasis is on making the observing system resilient, open, and strategically autonomous for Europe.

**#2 — Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This one is about *understanding and projecting* the future of the Antarctic/Southern Ocean region: ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice dynamics, improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models, monitoring indicators, and ecosystem vulnerability. It explicitly calls for work on extreme events, tipping points, and decadal-to-millennial projections.

**Which fits the project better?**

The project's slate is heavily weighted toward *forecasting and data assimilation* — ML-based marine heatwave forecasts (#8), operational ocean forecast systems (#13), and the practical use of forecasts to trigger rapid response for at-risk species (#7). That's a modelling-and-prediction orientation, not an infrastructure-deployment one.

On that basis, **#2 is the closer fit**. Its scope — improving regional coupled models, reducing uncertainty in projected changes, understanding extreme events, and developing monitoring indicators — lines up well with what the project is actually doing. The Antarctic/Southern Ocean focus is a narrower geographic frame, but the methodological core (model improvement, extreme-event understanding, monitoring) is the same muscle the project is building.

#11 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#16 [paper] Data‐Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing
Authors: Rafael Sebastian Reiss, Lisanne Blok, Nicholas Leonard, Kate Oglethorpe, Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, Colm-cille P. Caulfield, Ali Mashayek
Venue: Geophysical Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl123721
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic Ocean turbulent mixing is poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding, despite its importance for regional dynamics and global overturning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training gradient-boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data to predict turbulent dissipation from hydrographic variables, using spatial block cross-validation for evaluation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles) for training; pan-Arctic hydrographic observations and high-resolution model output for application.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

Authors: Minjong Cheon, Kaoru Kakinuma
Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational cost of Earth system models limits the exploration of scenarios and ensemble members, while existing machine-learning weather models coupled to oceans have produced weak El Niño variability or relied on climate-model output, and none effectively routes climate impacts through…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model using a coupler named YAHO that links a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon, and energy components constrained by observations; the model uses an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave oc…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Simulations of approximately 1,000 years on one graphics processing unit; evaluation against observed climate data from 1979-2022; routing of runoff to 212 river gauges; and future projections for SSP1 and SSP3 scenarios for the period 2081-2100.
Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

#30 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The interface of machine learning (ML) and data assimilation (DA), specifically how ML can be integrated with the process of combining model forecasts with observations to optimally estimate the state of chaotic systems such as the atmosphere.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Overview/survey of main topics and methods at the interface of ML and DA.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Operational forecasting centres worldwide, with particular emphasis on chaotic systems such as the atmosphere.
Abstract:
Data assimilation (DA) is the process of combining forecasts from a model with observations in order to optimally estimate the state of a system. This is critical for chaotic systems, such as the atmosphere, since if observations are not continually assimilated the model will quickly lose skill. DA is routinely performed (usually every 6 hours) at operational forecasting centres around the world. In this article we discuss the interface of machine learning (ML) and DA. This is still an emerging and quickly developing field, and this article tries to give an overview of some of the main topics and methods.

Authors: Simon S. Toedtli, D. Ahijevych, Wei Wang, C. Snyder
Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A two-way coupled DA system where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system uses the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar, cycled over one month.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A realistic DA cycling system assimilating a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances, over a one-month period.
Abstract:
Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances. We evaluate this capability in a two-way coupled DA system, where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system is cycled over one month and assimilates a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances. Using the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar yields ensemble spread and covariances comparable to a reference configuration in which MPAS evolves both components. The resulting EnVar mean achieves consistently lower RMSE against GFS analyses, except near the model top, where spurious correlations degrade performance. These results demonstrate that MLWP models can propagate covariance information in a realistic DA cycling system and provide a proof of concept for their integration into future operational ensemble systems.

Two open grants are on the Plastic pathways slate: #3 (€50M, EU, deadline 2027-02-16) and #10 (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15). **#3 is the better fit.**

The Plastic pathways project works on marine litter tracking, floating debris detection, satellite ocean remote sensing, Lagrangian particle tracking and beaching — i.e. it is fundamentally about *observing and tracking* what moves through the ocean. That maps directly onto #3's core aim of strengthening observing capacities and data coordination.
- **#10 (NSF OTIC)** is narrower: it funds *instrumentation development* with broad applicability to ocean science. The project's declared concepts are about tracking and remote sensing, not building new instruments, so the fit is weaker.

**Strongest reason:** the project's method (satellite remote sensing + Lagrangian tracking of debris) is exactly the kind of observing-capacity work #3 is built to fund. **Biggest doubt:** #3 is a very large, governance- and infrastructure-heavy call (€50M, GOOS/Copernicus framing, areas beyond national jurisdiction), so a single-lab plastic-pathways project would need to be framed as a component of a broader observing-system effort rather than a standalone study.

I have to be upfront: Mylo's confirmed state for this project is thin. What I can see is:

All three entered the slate this week (2026-11-10 to 11-13):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). A YOLO11-based detector/segmenter for low-contrast, curved ocean features in MODIS imagery. A data release of daily analyses from a regional ocean forecast system — the kind of daily flow-field product you'd drive particle tracking with. - **The biggest doubt:** OTIC is US-based (grants.gov), so eligibility depends on your institution's US affiliation or a US-based partner — I can't see your institution's location, so check that before committing.
- **The alternative if you're EU-based:** #3 (€50M GOOS call, deadline 2027-02-16) is a bigger, more infrastructure-oriented call — a stretch for a single project, but worth keeping in view if you're building a consortium. #12 (biodiversity data integration, €3–8M, deadline 2027-09-22) is the most distant fit of the three.

Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing

Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

The one that matters most is **#5 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, *Conservation Science and Practice*).

Why it stands out for your project:

- **It's the clearest example of an early-warning forecast actually triggering action.** Ahead of the 2023/24 El Niño, forecasts flagged a high risk of marine heatwaves; an expert workshop judged the forecasted extremes (>20°C or ~+3°C) a severe threat, and that triggered a pre-emptive rescue of 25 red handfish in January 2024. The heatwave then hit — 80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature — and the fish were released after it subsided, with post-release survival confirmed. That's the full loop your project is about: forecast → threshold → decision → verified outcome.
- **It gives you a concrete template for the "so what" of your warnings.** Most of the other papers on the slate are about building or evaluating the forecast itself; #5 shows what a forecast is *for* — a documented case where acting on it saved a critically endangered species. That's a strong anchor for framing the value of your early-warning system to managers and funders.
- **It's recent and published in a conservation venue**, so it's citable as evidence that forecast-triggered intervention is now an accepted practice, not a proposal.

The runner-up is **#6** (Mojumder, 2026), which is the closest methodological match — 1–14-day ML forecasts of marine heatwaves evaluated against persistence benchmarks, exactly the skill question your project has to answer. But it's a B.S. thesis dataset on Zenodo, so it's a useful benchmark to know about rather than a centerpiece. #3 (the Northeast Pacific seasonal forecast comment) is also relevant to the forecasting side, but it's about a seasonal system for resource management rather than heatwave early warning per se.

#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

The one that matters most for Plastic pathways is **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it stands out:

- **It is the only item on the slate that is directly about marine litter.** The others are about ocean observing systems, phytoplankton, ocean forecast models, or general remote sensing — related to the lab, but not to the project's core question of where plastic goes.
- **It tackles the exact hard part of pathway work: the last mile.** Most particle-tracking studies stop at the water–land boundary. This one builds a *tide-resolving beaching kernel* — a three-phase kernel for OceanParcels 3.1.4 — that handles how particles actually come ashore, validated against field records from Uido, Korea. That is precisely the kind of nearshore/stranding mechanism a plastic-pathways project needs to close the loop between open-ocean transport and where debris ends up.
- **It is immediately usable, not just a read.** The deposit includes the kernel code, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated result files behind every number in the manuscript — so it can be dropped into your own particle-tracking setup rather than just cited.

One caveat: it is the code/results deposit for a manuscript submitted to *Marine Pollution Bulletin*, so the full method discussion lives in that paper; the deposit gives you the machinery and the numbers.

If you want, I can pull the full text of the companion manuscript and walk through how the three-phase kernel works, or check whether the ROMS/OceanParcels setup in #7 is compatible with what your project currently runs.
